lesson.title: Protocols That Can Change: Protocol Versioning
lesson.summary: Protocol versioning is how a wire protocol keeps working correctly as it changes over time, letting old and new implementations either negotiate a common version or tolerate each other's differences instead of simply breaking.
lesson.body:
A wire protocol, once real implementations exist and are talking to each other, becomes very hard to change unilaterally. If a server changes its message format and a client is still using the old one, the two can no longer understand each other, and unlike a piece of software one team controls entirely, a protocol typically has many independent implementations, older client versions still installed on people's machines, other companies' software talking to a given service, that cannot all be upgraded in the same instant. Some way of evolving a protocol without breaking everyone still using an older version is close to a requirement for any protocol that expects to be used for more than a brief period.

The most direct approach is an explicit version field, somewhere early in the message, often in the very first bytes, that states which version of the protocol a message follows, for instance the HTTP/1.1 token that opens every HTTP request and response. When two sides connect, they can exchange or agree on a version explicitly, sometimes called version negotiation, where the client states the highest version it supports and the server responds with the version it will actually use, which might be lower if the server is older. This lets both sides settle on a version they both understand before doing anything else that depends on it.

Beyond a version number itself, well-designed protocols aim for backward and forward compatibility as far as reasonably possible. Backward compatibility means a newer implementation can still understand messages from an older version. Forward compatibility means an older implementation can still cope with messages from a newer version, typically not by fully understanding the new parts, but by safely ignoring fields or message types it does not recognize rather than treating them as an error. A common, deliberate design pattern that supports this is reserving space for future fields and specifying that unknown fields should be ignored rather than rejected, so that adding a new optional field to a message later does not break implementations written before that field existed. They simply skip over data they do not recognize and continue using what they do.

In practice, real protocols use a mix of these techniques. Some bump a major version number only for changes that genuinely break compatibility and expect both sides to explicitly negotiate down to a shared version when they differ, while making smaller, additive changes without a version bump at all, relying on the ignore-unknown-fields convention to keep things working. Getting this right is what allows something like a web server or a messaging system to keep serving traffic to a mix of old and new clients simultaneously during a rollout, rather than requiring every participant to upgrade in lockstep the instant anything changes, which for most real systems with independent clients is not something that can be guaranteed to happen anyway.
